name: Isnag
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Barlaan, Rodolfo R. 1995. "6. Isnag." In Darrell T. Tryon (ed.), Comparative Austronesian Dictionary: An Introduction to Austronesian Studies, Part 1, Fascicle 1 (Trends in Linguistics, Documentation 10), pp. 321-328. Berlin/New York: Mouton de Gruyter.
catalog_locator: p. 323, section 3 'Summary of the phonology', 3.1 'The syllable', 3.2 'Word stress', 3.3 'Length' (archive.org scan leaf 350)
catalog_quote: 3.1 The syllable. There are two syllable patterns in Isnag: (C)V and (C)VC. 3.2 Word stress. On the word level, stress is predictable. When long vowels including e and o which are always stressed are absent, the stress falls on the ultimate syllable. 3.3 Length. Length is contrastive in Isnag. Except for /e/ and /o/, all phonemes have their corresponding long forms. Long vowels are interpreted as one segment while long consonants are interpreted as geminate clusters.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not independently contrastive: a long vowel (and the mid vowels e and o, which count as long) always carries the stress; a word with no long vowel is stressed on its final syllable. Because vowel length is itself phonemic, stress position is predictable from the segmental (length) shape of the word rather than from a fixed syllable count; the default in the absence of length is word-final.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress. Related: 4.1.5 says that when two long vowels come to stand in adjacent syllables after affixation, the first is shortened (so a word does not keep two adjacent long, i.e. stressed, vowels).
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly 'on the word level'; sketch accompanies a citation-form wordlist. Data from the O? dialect, sub-dialect B, village of Dibagat above Kabugao (Glottolog dialect Dibagat-Kabugao diba1241). Blust 2013 (pp. 180-181, second-hand, from Vanoverbergh 1972 accent marks) treats Isneg as having lexical stress reflecting Proto-Philippine stress; the two views are compatible if Vanoverbergh's accent corresponds to Barlaan's contrastive length.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement comes from Barlaan's Isnag sketch in the Comparative Austronesian Dictionary (Tryon ed. 1995), whose data are from the O? dialect, sub-dialect B, village of Dibagat above Kabugao, i.e. Glottolog dialect Dibagat-Kabugao [diba1241] of Isnag [isna1241]; the source spells the language 'Isnag' and calls 'Isneg' a wrong spelling. Vanoverbergh's and Reid's works use 'Isneg' for the same language.

sources.note: Comparative remark only: Isneg is among the Philippine 'stress languages'; Isneg mata 'eye', lanit 'sky', dalan 'road' agree with Ilokano/Tagalog/Bikol in reflecting reconstructed PPH lexical stress, with 'language-specific differences in the conditions under which stress has been made predictable, as with Ilokano, Isneg, Bikol dalan'. No rule for Isneg stated; data from Vanoverbergh 1972 (fn. 5 p. 63 names it the major published source).

tone.quote: There are fifteen consonants: p, b, t, d, k, g, s, m, n, ng, l, r, w, y, and the glottal stop /ʔ/; six vowels: i, e, a, ʌ, u, and o; and stress. ... 5. Stress. The phoneme of stress has been observed to contrast in five pairs of words. ... Stressed syllables tend to be longer and lower in pitch than unstressed syllables. When words are given in isolation, stress may vary. The vowel in the penultimate open syllable is often lengthened, especially in question intonation.

tone.quote: [p. 1096] Note that [-long] is preassociated to the V slot. ... [p. 1098] The derivation of diminutives presents an interesting problem of apparent overapplication of the shortening rule (represented autosegmentally as the preattached feature [-long] in the reduplicating prefix). The [-long] feature is found not only in the reduplicated prefix but also in the stem; the diminutive form for tolay 'person' is tultulay 'a very small person'. ... [p. 1103, note 5] In Isnag o is always long. When shortened it is raised to u.
tone.locator: p. 1095 (end of 'Plurals') for 'Note that [-long] is preassociated to the V slot.'; p. 1098 ('Diminutives') for the overapplication passage; p. 1103 (Notes, n. 5) for 'In Isnag o is always long. When shortened it is raised to u.', so C's 'p. 1096' is one page late; likewise note 1 (identity passage) is on p. 1102, notes 2-6 on p. 1103.

tone.quote: In Philippine languages, vowel length (or shortness) is the most important feature of word accent—for various historical reasons, also because of intonation (which can override pitch and stress). [p. 18] ... Table 2. Accent classification of Austronesian languages (A) Phonemic length and shortness, as inherited from PPH (< PHN, PMP, PAN): Bisayan (except Kuyonon and Tausug), Coastal and Pandan Bikol, Balangaw, Bontok, Hanunoo, Ifugao, Ilokano, Isneg, Itneg, Itawit, Kalinga, Kapampangan, Kankanay, Malaweg, Sambal, Tagalog. [p. 20] ... (F) Consonant length (1: gemination, or 2: strengthening) following a short vowel (generally, but not always *e): Bagobo, Ilokano, Kagayanen, Obo, Isneg, Itneg, Malaweg, Tagabawa, Madurese, Buginese, Sama-Bajaw. [p. 21]
